title: The Smoke-Filled Room
text:
In 1968, at Columbia University, Bibb Latane and John Darley asked students to sit in a small room and fill in a questionnaire. A few minutes later, white smoke began to puff through a vent in the wall. It kept coming until the room was hazy and hard to see through.

When students were alone, most of them soon got up, looked at the vent and went to report the smoke. About three quarters did so within the six minutes the experiment allowed.

In another condition, the student sat with two other people who were working for the researchers. They noticed the smoke, shrugged and kept writing. In that situation only about one in ten real participants reported it. Most sat coughing and waving smoke away, glancing at the others, and carried on with the questionnaire. Even when three genuine participants sat together, the room was reported far less often than when people were alone.

Afterward, those who had stayed put explained the smoke away as steam, air conditioning vapor or a truth gas. Each person had looked to the others to judge whether there was danger, and the others, doing the same, seemed calm.
lesson: A calm group can be a group where everyone is waiting for someone else. If something looks wrong, say so out loud rather than reading safety from other people's faces.
source: Latane, B., and Darley, J. M. (1968). Group inhibition of bystander intervention in emergencies. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 10(3), 215-221.
